title: Type Casting
description: Moving a value from one type to another, and the whole-number division trap.

items.title: Widening: automatic
items.text: Every whole number is also a decimal. Nothing can be lost.

items.title: Narrowing: needs a cast
items.code:
double price = 7.9;
int n = price;      // error
items.text: An `int` cannot hold .9, so Java stops: `possible lossy conversion`.

content.value: To narrow anyway, write a **cast**: the target type in round brackets before the value. It tells Java: I know, do it anyway.

content.caption: 7.9 became 7, not 8. A cast to `int` cuts off the decimal part. Real rounding uses `Math.round`, in Module 6.

content.question: What is `(int) -2.7`?
content.explain: A cast to `int` throws the decimal part away. It never rounds, so -2.7 becomes -2.

content.value: When both sides of `/` are `int`, Java does whole-number division: it throws the remainder away straight away.

steps.note: Both sides of the coming division are `int`.
One side is a `double`, so the answer keeps its fraction.
Not a fix: `7 / 2` is worked out as 3 first, then widened to 3.0.
The cast turns 7 into 7.0 before dividing. Fixed in time.
The type on the left could not repair it.
Casting one side gives the real answer.

content.title: Where the 0.5 goes

content.value: Percentages bite hardest. `correct * 100 / total` loses the fraction. `correct * 100.0 / total` keeps it.
content.title: Percentages

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so Java divides in whole numbers and drops the .5.

content.value: A `char` is stored as a number code. `'A'` is 65. So a `char` widens into an `int`, and an `int` casts back to a `char`.

content.title: Same letter, two views
content.caption: Adding two chars adds their codes: `'A' + 'B'` is 131. Join them as text with `"" + 'A' + 'B'`.

items.title: Cast: error
items.text: `String` is not related to the number types. Text is still text.

items.title: Parse: works
items.text: **Parsing** reads the characters and works out the number.

content.caption: `number` really is an `int`, so `+ 8` adds: 50, not 428. Module 3 parses every number a person types.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `Integer.parseInt` turns the text into the number 5, so `+ 1` is real addition.

practice.question: Store 9.7 in a `double`, then print both the original and the value cast to an `int`. Check that it chops rather than rounds.
A student scored 17 out of 20. Both are `int`. Print the percentage as a `double`, so it reads 85.0 and not 85 or 0.
This program prints 3.0 when it should print 3.3333333333333335. Fix it with one cast.

quiz.question: Why does `double d = 7;` compile without a cast?
options: It is widening: an int fits inside a double, so nothing can be lost.
Java ignores types when the number is small.
quiz.explain: Every whole number is a valid decimal number, so the move is safe and Java does it automatically. It stores 7.0.

quiz.question: What does `(int) 7.9` give?
options: 7, because a cast chops the decimal part off
8, because it rounds to the nearest whole number
quiz.explain: Casting to `int` throws the fractional part away rather than rounding. For rounding you need `Math.round`, which comes in Module 6.

quiz.question: What does `System.out.println(7 / 2);` print?
quiz.explain: Both values are `int`, so Java does whole-number division and drops the remainder. Making either side a `double` gives 3.5.

quiz.question: Does `double answer = 7 / 2;` fix that problem?
options: No: the division happens first as ints, so it stores 3.0.
Yes: the type on the left makes it a decimal division.
No: it does not compile at all.
quiz.explain: The right hand side is worked out before anything is stored, so 3 is produced and then widened to 3.0. Cast one side of the division instead.

quiz.question: How do you turn the text `"42"` into the number 42?
options: You cannot: text can never become a number.
quiz.explain: A cast only works between related types, and `String` is not a number type. Parsing reads the characters and works out the value they spell.

quiz.question: What is `(char) 66` if `'A'` has code 65?
quiz.explain: Characters are stored as codes, so the code one after `'A'` is `'B'`. Casting an `int` to a `char` looks up the character with that code.
